newsitem.title: UK: UK drug industry wants bigger health budget.
newsitem.headline: UK drug industry wants bigger health budget.

text.p: Britain's pharmaceutical industry said on Monday that the next government should increase UK spending on health by at least half a percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

Launching its own manifesto for the next general election the Pharmaceutical Industry Council, an umbrella group representing different trade bodies, also called on the new government to tackle concerns about science education and the dwindling British science base.

Trevor Jones, director general of the Association of the British Pharmaceutical Industry (ABPI), told a news conference that "the percentage spent on health and research and development (in Britain) is lower than many European countries and other developed world economies."
The UK spends around 6.6 percent of GDP on health, far less than countries like the U.S. and France.

He said a new government should "make a movement in that direction of at least half a percent." The industry also argues that more money spent on drug treatment would reduce spending on keeping people in hospital.
The ABPI, which represents more than 100 prescription drug makers in Britain, is one of 15 groups which put their name to the document, entitled "What Industry Needs From Government."

With the opposition Labour Party more than 20 points ahead in opinion polls, the move wil be seen as a pre-emptive strike against a possible Labour government. The Labour Party has historically been less friendly towards the drugs industry than the ruling Conservatives. The next general election must be held by May 22.

The ABPI's Jones said even though Labour's finance spokesman and putative Chancellor Gordon Brown appeared to have a "tough" approach to spending, the industry would expect a Labour government to reorder its spending priorities.
"For a party that is so declaredly in favour of social welfare and health an element of that redirection should come the way of health," he said.
The Council also repeated the industry's opposition to the Prodigy computer software system, which gives doctors a narrow choice of the drugs thay can prescribe for different conditions.
And it expressed concern that a future government might allow pharmacists to substitute cheaper, generic drugs where a doctor has prescribed a branded product. This is illegal at present.

The industry said it also wanted to hold talks on the future of prescription charges. It believes the 550 pence flat-fee charge deters some people from getting the medicines that doctors prescribe and bears no relation to the cost of a drug.
"We have had no clarity from the Labour Party on their view of prescription charges," ABPI's Jones said. "We have had clarity from the government because they have just put them up."

Sheila Kelly of the Proprietary Association of Great Britain, which represents over-the-counter medicine makers, expressed concern about the possible abolition of fixed prices for over-the-counter drugs, which she said threatened the survival of many community pharmacies.
